summary.text: Assuming either family is finite, choose a bound \(N\ge5\) (enlarged by \(2\) when bounding the upper member of a twin pair), set \(n=(N+1)!/6\), and use positivity to obtain \((N+1)!=p+q\), where \(p=6x-1\) is Sophie Germain and \(q=6y+1\) is the upper twin prime. In each case the bounded relevant prime summand is at most \(N\), so it divides \((N+1)!\) and hence the other prime summand; it must therefore equal that summand, forcing \((N+1)!\le2N\), contrary to \((N+1)!>2N\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs. Thus infinitude of \(\mathcal T\) is exactly infinitude of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is the sum, over integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of an indicator which is \(1\) precisely when all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6(n-x)-1,\qquad 6(n-x)+1
\]
are prime. Consequently, if \(a(n)>0\), at least one summand is nonzero. Hence there is an integer \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\) such that all four displayed numbers are prime. Put
\[
y=n-x.
\]
Because \(x<n\), we have \(y\ge 1\), and of course \(n=x+y\). If
\[
p=6x-1,
\]
then
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
so \(p\in\mathcal S\). If
\[
r=6y-1,
\]
then \(r+2=6y+1\), so \(r\in\mathcal T\). We shall repeatedly use the identity
\[
6n=6(x+y)=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+(r+2). \tag{1}
\]

Assume throughout the conjectural positivity hypothesis
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1. \tag{2}
\]
We prove separately that \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) are infinite.

We first record the elementary factorial estimate used in both parts. For every integer \(N\ge5\),
\[
(N+1)!>2N. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(N+1)!=(N+1)N(N-1)!.
\]
Since \(N\ge5\), monotonicity of factorial gives
\[
(N-1)!\ge4!=24.
\]
In particular \((N+1)(N-1)!>2\). Multiplying this strict inequality by the positive integer \(N\) yields (3).

### Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

Suppose, for a contradiction, that \(\mathcal S\) is finite. Every finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound, so choose \(M\) such that
\[
p\le M\qquad\text{for every }p\in\mathcal S. \tag{4}
\]
Let
\[
N=\max\{5,M\}.
\]
Then \(N\ge5\), \(N\ge M\), and \(N+1\ge6\). Since every positive integer at most \(N+1\) divides \((N+1)!\), in particular
\[
6\mid (N+1)!.
\]
Thus
\[
n=\frac{(N+1)!}{6}
\]
is an integer and
\[
6n=(N+1)!. \tag{5}
\]
Moreover, by (3),
\[
6n=(N+1)!>2N\ge10,
\]
so \(n>1\).

Apply (2) to this \(n\). By the extraction argument above, there are positive integers \(x,y\), with \(n=x+y\), such that
\[
p=6x-1
\]
is a Sophie Germain prime and
\[
r=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1=r+2
\]
are twin primes. Since \(p\in\mathcal S\), (4) and the choice of \(N\) give
\[
p\le M\le N<N+1. \tag{6}
\]
Also \(p>0\), in fact \(p\ge5\), because \(x\ge1\). It follows from (6) that \(p\) is one of the positive integers occurring among the factors of \((N+1)!\), and therefore
\[
p\mid (N+1)!. \tag{7}
\]
On the other hand, equations (1) and (5) give
\[
(N+1)!=p+q. \tag{8}
\]
Since \(p\mid(N+1)!\) and \(p\mid p\), subtracting the latter divisible summand from (8) shows that
\[
p\mid q. \tag{9}
\]
The number \(q=6y+1\) is prime. A positive divisor of a prime is either \(1\) or the prime itself. Thus (9) gives the two cases
\[
p=1\quad\text{or}\quad p=q.
\]
The first case is impossible because \(x\ge1\) implies \(p=6x-1\ge5\). Hence
\[
p=q.
\]
Using (8) and (6), we now obtain
\[
(N+1)!=p+q=2p\le2N,
\]
contradicting the strict factorial estimate (3). Therefore \(\mathcal S\) cannot be finite, so there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.

### Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Suppose now, again for a contradiction, that \(\mathcal T\) is finite. Choose an upper bound \(M\) for its elements, so that
\[
r\le M\qquad\text{for every }r\in\mathcal T. \tag{10}
\]
Here \(r\) denotes the lower prime in a twin-prime pair. Set
\[
N=\max\{5,M+2\}.
\]
Then \(N\ge5\) and \(N\ge M+2\). As before, \(N+1\ge6\), so \(6\mid(N+1)!\). Define
\[
n=\frac{(N+1)!}{6}.
\]
Then
\[
6n=(N+1)!, \tag{11}
\]
and (3) again implies \(6n>2N\ge10\), hence \(n>1\).

By (2), choose positive integers \(x,y\) with \(n=x+y\) for which
\[
p=6x-1
\]
is prime (indeed, it is a Sophie Germain prime), and
\[
r=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1=r+2
\]
are both prime. The lower member \(r\) belongs to \(\mathcal T\), so (10) yields
\[
r\le M.
\]
Consequently the upper member satisfies
\[
q=r+2\le M+2\le N. \tag{12}
\]
Since \(q>0\) and \(q\le N<N+1\), it follows that
\[
q\mid(N+1)!. \tag{13}
\]
Using \(n=x+y\), equations (1) and (11) say
\[
(N+1)!=p+q. \tag{14}
\]
Now (13), together with the obvious divisibility \(q\mid q\), implies after subtracting the second summand in (14) that
\[
q\mid p. \tag{15}
\]
The number \(p=6x-1\) is prime. Therefore its positive divisor \(q\) must satisfy
\[
q=1\quad\text{or}\quad q=p.
\]
The first case is impossible: since \(y\ge1\),
\[
q=6y+1\ge7.
\]
Thus \(q=p\). From (14) and (12) we conclude
\[
(N+1)!=p+q=2q\le2N,
\]
again contradicting (3). Hence \(\mathcal T\) is infinite.

We have proved that the positivity of \(A227923(n)\) for every \(n>1\) forces both \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) to be infinite. In other words, there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
